summary: Peru grants visa-free entry to citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas — 90 days, extendable once by 90 days within a year, for most of them, and 90 days in any 180 for EU and Schengen-area passports other than Ireland's — records arrivals by air digitally, and lets Chinese and Indian citizens who hold a US, UK, Canadian, Australian or Schengen visa valid for at least six months, or permanent residence in one of those countries, enter without a Peruvian visa.

CN.notes: Peru's visa-exemption table: citizens of China and India with valid ordinary passports can enter Peru without a temporary tourist visa if they show at least one of these: a) a visa valid for at least six (6) months from the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia or a Schengen Area state; b) permanent residence in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia or a Schengen Area state.

source.name: Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores del Perú — Requerimientos y exoneración de visas para ciudadanos extranjeros con pasaportes ordinarios (16 July 2026)

quote.text: Los ciudadanos de China e India que posean pasaportes ordinarios válidos y vigentes pueden ingresar al Perú sin visa temporal de turista, siempre que acrediten al menos una de las siguientes condiciones: a) Ser titulares de visas con una vigencia mínima de seis (6) meses de los Estados Unidos de América, Canadá, Reino Unido de Gran Bretaña e Irlanda del Norte, Australia o de un Estado perteneciente al Espacio Schengen. b) Tener residencia permanente en los Estados Unidos de América, Canadá, Reino Unido de Gran Bretaña e Irlanda del Norte, Australia o en un Estado perteneciente al Espacio Schengen.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: WHO lists no yellow fever requirement at entry to Peru; Peru's health ministry says travellers heading to jungle areas should be vaccinated at least 10 days before the trip. The endemic areas are the forested jungle of Loreto, Madre de Dios, San Martín, Ucayali and Amazonas and the jungle zones of Junín, Ayacucho, Cusco, Huánuco, Pasco and Puno — Machu Picchu and the Inca Trail are excluded.

notes: Canada's travel advice says Peru's international airports do not stamp passports and keep digital entry and exit records instead; Migraciones says you can check your authorized stay by downloading your virtual Andean Migration Card (TAM).
The UK government says it is illegal to remove any archaeological artefacts from Peru without authorisation.
The UK government advises against taking coca leaves or coca tea out of Peru, as importing them into the UK is illegal.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says street crime, including muggings and thefts, is a significant problem in Lima, Cusco, Arequipa and other major cities; that tourists, especially those travelling alone, are at risk of 'express kidnapping', often by criminals posing as taxi drivers; and that the border areas with Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil and the VRAEM carry a higher risk because of organised crime linked to drug production. It advises licensed telephone or app-based taxis rather than hailing one on the street.

tips.text: The UK government says altitude sickness is a serious risk in parts of Peru, including Cusco, Puno, the Colca Canyon and Kuelap. Canada's travel advice says the risk starts at 2,500 metres and is higher if you ascend quickly or exercise or drink alcohol before you get used to the altitude.

The UK government warns of robberies by criminals posing as taxi drivers, especially at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport and bus terminals, and advises licensed telephone or app-based taxis, hotel-booked taxis, or the official taxi desks outside the airport baggage hall.
Australia's Smartraveller advises drinking boiled or bottled water in Peru.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Peru?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter Peru visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days, extendable once for another 90 days within 365 days of first entry. Canada's travel advice says entry by air is recorded digitally rather than stamped in the passport.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Peru as a tourist?
faq.answer: It depends on your passport. Most visa-exempt visitors get 90 days, extendable once for another 90 days within 365 days of first entry; EU and Schengen-area passports other than Ireland's (and those of Georgia, Russia, Turkey and Ukraine) get 90 days in any 180-day period; Mexico, El Salvador and Qatar get 183 days, Barbados, Costa Rica, Honduras and Panama 90 days, and the Dominican Republic 60 days, none of them extendable.

faq.question: Do Chinese or Indian citizens need a visa for Peru?
faq.answer: Yes, a consular tourist visa, unless you meet the following condition: as a Chinese or Indian citizen holding a US, UK, Canadian, Australian or Schengen visa valid for at least six months (or permanent residence in those places) you can enter Peru without a Peruvian visa for tourism or business, for up to 180 days within 365 days of first entry, not extendable.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccine for Machu Picchu or the Amazon?
faq.answer: Not for Machu Picchu or the Inca Trail, which Peru's health ministry excludes. It recommends vaccination at least 10 days before travel to jungle areas: the forested jungle of Loreto, Madre de Dios, San Martín, Ucayali and Amazonas and the jungle zones of Junín, Ayacucho, Cusco region, Huánuco, Pasco and Puno.

faq.question: Do I need to fill in an entry form (TAM) for Peru?
faq.answer: No official source we could read describes an entry form to fill in. Canada's travel advice says Peru's international airports keep digital entry and exit records instead of stamping passports, and Migraciones says you can check your authorized stay by downloading your virtual Andean Migration Card (TAM).
